lesson.title: Sharing Is Bonding: What Bonding Pairs Really Are
lesson.summary: A bonding pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms that holds them together in a covalent bond, and counting bonding pairs correctly is the backbone of drawing an accurate Lewis structure.
lesson.body:
A bonding pair, also called a shared pair, is any pair of electrons that sits between two atomic nuclei and is counted toward both atoms' octets at once. In a Lewis structure a bonding pair is drawn as a single line connecting two atom symbols, or less commonly as two dots between them. Bonding pairs are what actually hold atoms together: the shared electrons are attracted to both positive nuclei simultaneously, and that mutual attraction is the covalent bond itself.

The number of bonding pairs between two atoms tells you the bond type. One shared pair is a single bond, two shared pairs make a double bond, and three shared pairs make a triple bond, each drawn with one, two, or three lines respectively. Methane, CH4, is a simple molecule made entirely of bonding pairs. Carbon contributes 4 valence electrons and each of the four hydrogens contributes 1, for a total of 8. All 8 electrons are used to form four C-H bonding pairs, one to each hydrogen, and carbon ends up with a full octet made up entirely of bonding pairs and no lone pairs at all.

Compare that to water, where oxygen has two bonding pairs, to the two hydrogens, plus two lone pairs. The total number of electron pairs around an atom, bonding pairs plus lone pairs, is what determines its electron geometry, a connection that becomes central once you study molecular shapes. For now, the key skill is counting correctly: every bonding pair uses 2 of the molecule's total valence electrons, and every atom involved in that bond gets to count both electrons toward its own octet, which is why a single shared pair can satisfy two atoms' requirements simultaneously instead of just one.

Carbon dioxide, CO2, is a useful example with multiple bonding pairs of different types. Total valence electrons: carbon contributes 4, and each oxygen contributes 6, for 4 plus 12, or 16. The structure O=C=O has two double bonds, meaning two bonding pairs connect carbon to each oxygen, for four bonding pairs total, 8 electrons, plus two lone pairs on each oxygen, 8 more electrons, for 16 electrons overall. Carbon has no lone pairs and gets its full octet entirely from its four bonding pairs, since 2 double bonds times 4 electrons each, counted toward carbon, equals 8.

Distinguishing bonding pairs from lone pairs is not just bookkeeping. It sets up nearly every topic ahead: formal charge depends on how many electrons in a bond belong to each atom, resonance structures differ in exactly where bonding pairs, not atoms, are placed, and molecular geometry depends on the total count of both pair types around a central atom. Getting comfortable identifying bonding pairs at a glance, versus lone pairs sitting on a single atom, is one of the most transferable skills in a Lewis structure toolkit. A quick way to check your work on any Lewis structure is to add up all bonding pair electrons and all lone pair electrons and confirm the sum equals the molecule's total valence electron count, the same total you calculated before placing a single bond.
